publication_posture: Historical engineering reference and educational field manual. It explains ROB's hand-built evolution and gives readers methods for studying or recreating its ideas, but it is not dimensionally complete CAD, a stamped design, a certified construction plan, or proof that the current machine is safe to reproduce. Missing as-built CAD is identified as future documentation work.

identity.rob_name_meaning: ROB is a friendly name derived from the word robot; it is not an acronym.
identity.origin_context: The physical project began after Rodolfo Aramayo left Verizon Labs, where he had worked as a systems software engineer on mobile VR/AR research technologies. The surviving 2017-2018 Cerebro serial-control work belongs to ROB's initial hardware prototype.
identity.initial_inspiration: The author wanted to bring the friendly, expressive idea of the movie robot Johnny 5 into an era of mobile devices and 3D depth cameras. This is personal historical inspiration, not a claim of affiliation or a license to copy the character or film design.
identity.original_mission: Build an expressive mobile robot around modern mobile interfaces, depth sensing, speech, and experimental conversational software. The early software included a local CakeChat neural-dialogue experiment that predates ChatGPT; CakeChat is not described as a technical ancestor of ChatGPT.
identity.current_mission: ROB is the author's career-scale personal engineering platform: the most elaborate project of his career and a continuing way to stretch his mobile, spatial-computing, robotics, perception, and AI-development skills while teaching others from the evidence.
identity.cerebro_name_story: Cerebro is a playful reference to cognition and the brain: the macOS application acts as ROB's coordinating processing center without claiming human consciousness.
identity.rob_makina_name_story: Rob Makina was the author's wordplay for robot machine, using a Latin-sounding construction in early source headers; it was a project persona, not a separate contributor.
identity.cerebro_v5_migration_reason: The August 2025 v5 repository was a pragmatic clean-history migration. The author considered the older repository cluttered by long history and artifacts, so he started a new repository from the then-current application. The reset was a version-control choice, not Cerebro's beginning.

history.contributors_and_roles: Rodolfo Aramayo identifies himself as the sole builder, author, and principal software developer. Product suppliers and manufacturers are credited for components, not as co-builders or endorsers: Apple (Mac mini), Arashi Vision/Insta360 (Insta360 Pro II), HengDrive (motors), B-COMMAND (custom rotary/slip-ring interfaces), NETGEAR (Orbi networking), AMBER Robotics (B1 arms and controller environment), SuperDroid Robots (LT2 tread system), Arduino (Mega 2560 controller platform), and SLAMTEC/SLAMWARE (RPLIDAR mapping stack), plus other suppliers identified in the component record.
history.public_demonstrations: Official Maker Faire records identify R.O.B. as an exhibit at Maker Faire Bay Area 2019 (May 17-19, San Mateo County Event Center, San Mateo, California), as a Bay Area project in 2023 (the event ran October 13-15 and 20-22 at Mare Island Naval Shipyard, Vallejo), at Maker Faire Bay Area 2024 (October 18-20 at Mare Island), and at Maker Faire Bay Area 2025 (September 26-28 at Mare Island). The 2026 fair is scheduled for September 25-27, after this August 29 publication record; no 2026 R.O.B. appearance is claimed without a later accepted-project or post-event record.
history.major_failures_repairs_and_revisions: The first prototype used a car battery, Power Wheels motors and wheels, scrap wood, an older Intel laptop, and an old robotic arm. ROB then moved to a SuperDroid Robots LT2 tracked base with a third-wheel/flipper idea intended to help turning and stair experiments. Early roughly 30 W brushless motors were underpowered at 12 V; gearing changes recovered torque but not the desired speed, and a 12-to-24 V boost stage made the robot stronger and faster while it remained slow and high-torque. Later revisions added RPLIDAR, a stepper-driven torso, and a Maestro-controlled hobby-servo arm and plastic gripper system with recordable actions. Heavy AMBER B1 arms introduced a long integration period because the original single-arm controller environment did not provide the desired coordinated dual-arm operation. The author later purchased a dedicated dual-arm B1 setup for approximately $22,500. Recent AI-assisted work expanded secure controllers, Vision Pro H.264 camera viewing, depth-camera integration, machine vision, Gemini and Apple-model experiments, voice/video input, and the modern ROBController and Cerebro feature set. These are historical recollections; dimensions, ratings, and safety claims remain governed by measured evidence.
